clips.title: Greece was twice as rich as Poland in 2008. Not anymore #Shorts
clips.desc: 2008: $31.7k vs $14.0k per person. 2024: Poland passed Greece. 2025: Croatia too (World Bank).

clips.title: 12 EU countries passed Greece since 2008 #Shorts
clips.desc: Adjusted for prices (Eurostat PPS), only Bulgaria is still behind Greece in the EU.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · GDP per capita (current US$)
shots.narration: In 2008, the average Greek produced almost thirty-two thousand dollars a year. The average Pole, about fourteen thousand. {p} Greece was more than twice as rich. It had joined the euro in 2001, and hosted the Olympics in 2004. {pp} In 2024, Poland passed Greece for the first time. {p} In 2025, Croatia did too, by a hair. {p} The average Pole now produces about twenty-eight and a half thousand dollars a year. The average Croatian, about twenty-seven thousand one hundred. The average Greek, just under twenty-seven thousand.

shots.src: Eurostat prc_ppp_ind · GDP per capita in PPS (EU27 = 100), 2000–2024
shots.title: Who passed Greece since 2008
shots.narration: Adjusted for prices, it's even more dramatic. {p} In 2008, Greece was richer than thirteen other EU countries. {p} Since then, twelve of them have passed it: Czechia and Malta in 2010. Portugal, Slovakia and Slovenia in 2011. Estonia in 2012. Lithuania in 2013. Poland and Hungary in 2015. Romania and Croatia in 2019. Latvia in 2020. {pp} Today, by this measure, only one country in the European Union is poorer than Greece: Bulgaria.

So how did one of Europe's richer countries fall to second-to-last? {p} And how did Poland, which spent the 1980s under communism, climb past it? {pp} <soft>It's a story about a crash, a rescue, and a comeback most people missed.</soft>

shots.src: World Bank WDI · GDP per capita, PPP (constant 2021 international $), change since 2008
shots.narration: Greece's crash began with a number nobody believed. {p} In late 2009, a new government admitted that the budget deficit was far bigger than reported: more than double the official figure. {p} Lenders panicked, and Greece could no longer borrow. {pp} Ireland, Portugal, Spain and Cyprus all needed help in those years too. But Greece fell furthest: one of the deepest peacetime collapses of any rich country since the Second World War. {p} By 2013, Greek output per person, after inflation, was down about a quarter from 2008. {p} It still hasn't fully recovered: in 2025, it was about eight percent below its 2008 level. {p} Poland's grew about eighty-four percent.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · unemployment, total and youth (% of labor force, modeled ILO estimate) · GDP growth (annual %)
shots.narration: Then came the jobs. {p} In 2013, more than one in four Greeks who wanted work couldn't find it: about twenty-eight percent. Among young people, almost six in ten. Imagine a whole generation leaving school with almost no jobs to go to. {p} The economy shrank for five years in a row, from 2009 to 2013. In 2011 alone, by almost ten percent. {pp} Poland, meanwhile, did something no other country in the European Union managed: in 2009, the worst year of the global financial crisis, its economy still grew. Every other EU economy shrank.

shots.src: European Stability Mechanism: Greek programmes 2010, 2012, 2015 (EU loans + IMF ≈ €289 billion, the largest financial assistance package in history) · Eurostat gov_10dd_edpt1 (general government gross debt, % of GDP)
shots.title: The Greek rescue
shots.narration: To avoid bankruptcy, Greece took three rescue packages from the rest of Europe and the IMF, in 2010, 2012 and 2015: almost two hundred and ninety billion euros in loans. {p} It was the largest financial rescue in history. {p} In return, Greece had to cut pensions and wages, raise taxes, and sell state assets. {p} In the summer of 2015, banks closed for three weeks, and people could take out only sixty euros a day. {pp} Even so, its government debt kept climbing, to more than two hundred percent of the economy by 2020.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · gross fixed capital formation (% of GDP)
shots.narration: The cuts hit the thing that builds a country's future: investment. Without it, workers can't become more productive, and wages can't rise for long. {p} Before the crisis, Greece invested about the same share of its economy as Poland and the EU average: around twenty-three percent. {p} For most of the 2010s, it invested about eleven percent, the lowest in the European Union. Fewer new factories, machines, roads and offices. {pp} Poland, Croatia and Romania were pouring money, much of it from EU funds, into new motorways, railways and factories. {p} Today, Croatia and Romania still invest about a quarter of their economies every year. Greece, about seventeen percent.
Quick favor: if you're enjoying this, hit subscribe. One country passing another, with the real numbers, every day. {p} Now, here's where Greeks actually feel all this: the paycheck.

shots.src: Eurostat earn_mw_cur · monthly minimum wage (EUR), January
shots.narration: In 2008, Greece's minimum wage was about seven hundred and ninety euros a month. Poland's, about three hundred and forty. {p} Then, in 2012, as part of the rescue, Greece cut its minimum wage by more than a fifth. {p} Poland's kept rising, year after year. {pp} In 2025, Poland's minimum wage was about eleven hundred euros a month. Greece's, about a thousand and thirty. {p} Croatia's, about nine hundred and seventy, is right behind. {p} And that's before adjusting for prices. Things cost less in Poland than in Greece, so a Polish minimum wage goes even further.

shots.title: Greece's population since 2011
shots.narration: And many Greeks voted with their feet. {p} Since 2011, Greece's population has fallen by almost seven hundred thousand people, about one in sixteen. {p} Many of those who left were young and educated, and went to work in Germany, Britain and the Netherlands. {pp} A country that loses its young workers loses its future taxpayers too. And fewer workers means slower growth, which makes catching up even harder.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · life expectancy at birth, total (years), 2024
shots.title: Life expectancy, 2024
shots.narration: But here's the twist: Greece is still a very good place to live. {p} Greeks live about eighty-two years on average. {pp} Poles, about seventy-eight. {p} That's almost three and a half years more, in the country that's supposedly poorer. {p} Greeks also consume more than their output suggests. Adjusted for prices, what the average Greek actually consumes is about eighty-one percent of the EU average, well above Greece's output, at seventy.

shots.src: Eurostat gov_10dd_edpt1 · government debt and budget balance (% of GDP) · World Bank WDI · GDP growth (annual %)
shots.narration: And Greece's comeback has quietly begun. {p} Since 2021, the Greek economy has grown faster than the EU average every single year. {p} Its government now runs a budget surplus: in 2025, about two percent of the economy. Poland ran a deficit of about seven percent, one of the largest in the EU. {pp} And Greek debt is falling: from more than two hundred percent of the economy in 2020, to about a hundred and forty-five percent in 2025. Still the highest in the EU, but down by more than sixty points in five years.
So Greece isn't collapsing anymore. It's recovering. {p} The problem is that its neighbors are recovering faster. {pp} In 2025, Poland grew about three and a half percent. Greece, about two.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · GDP per capita, PPP (current international $) · Eurostat prc_ppp_ind · GDP per capita in PPS (EU27 = 100)
shots.narration: So who's next? {p} Adjusted for prices, Bulgaria is the only EU country still behind Greece. And by the World Bank's measure, it's now within about two percent. {p} In 2000, Greece produced almost three times as much per person as Bulgaria, at those prices. {pp} If Bulgaria keeps growing faster, Greece could soon be last in the European Union. Romania already passed it, back in 2019. {p} And Bulgaria just joined the euro, in January 2026: the same club Greece joined twenty-five years earlier.

So is Poland really richer than Greece now? {p} In dollars, yes, since 2024. Adjusted for prices, yes, since 2015. {p} In how long people live, Greece is still clearly ahead. {p} But the bigger story isn't Greece falling. It's Eastern Europe rising. {p} Twenty years ago, these countries were the EU's poor relatives. Today, they're passing the old South, one by one. Portugal and Greece have already been passed. Others may be next. {pp} <soft>Which country do you think Poland passes next?</soft> Tell me in the comments.
Greece wasn't the only one. Poland passed Portugal too. To see how, watch this next. {p} I'm Chartbound. See you in the next one.

yt.title: In 2008, Greece Was Twice as Rich as Poland. Now It's Behind.
yt.description:
In 2008 the average Greek produced more than twice as much as the average Pole, in dollars. In 2024 Poland passed Greece, and in 2025 Croatia did too. Adjusted for prices, 12 of the 13 EU countries that were poorer than Greece in 2008 have passed it; only Bulgaria is still behind. The crash, the €289 billion rescue, the paycheck, and the twist: Greeks still live longer, run a budget surplus and are growing again.

Sources: World Bank WDI (NY.GDP.PCAP.CD, NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.CD, NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD, NY.GDP.MKTP.KD.ZG, NE.GDI.FTOT.ZS, SL.UEM.TOTL.ZS, SL.UEM.1524.ZS, SP.POP.TOTL, SP.DYN.LE00.IN); Eurostat (prc_ppp_ind, earn_mw_cur, gov_10dd_edpt1); European Stability Mechanism (Greek programmes 2010–2018).
